Discrete cosine and sine transforms

Source: R/r2r.R
fft_dct.Rd

fft_dct() and fft_dst() compute discrete cosine and sine transforms of types 1 to 4, or their inverses, over any subset of the dimensions of an array. The definitions, scaling and orthogonalize behaviour are those of scipy.fft.dct(), dctn(), dst() and dstn().

Usage

fft_dct(
  x,
  type = 2L,
  inverse = FALSE,
  n = NULL,
  axes = NULL,
  norm = c("backward", "ortho", "forward", "none"),
  orthogonalize = NULL,
  workers = NULL
)

fft_dst(
  x,
  type = 2L,
  inverse = FALSE,
  n = NULL,
  axes = NULL,
  norm = c("backward", "ortho", "forward", "none"),
  orthogonalize = NULL,
  workers = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A double, integer, logical or complex vector or array. Complex input is transformed as its real and imaginary parts separately.

type

The transform type: 1, 2, 3 or 4.

inverse

TRUE for the inverse transform.

n

Transform lengths, one per transformed axis in the order of axes (no recycling); with axes = NULL, one per dimension, in dimension order. Each axis of x is cropped or zero-padded to its length first. NULL keeps the lengths of x. For fft_c2r(), n gives the lengths of the real output; the halved axis of x must then hold n %/% 2 + 1 values and is cropped or padded to that. Its default is 2 * (m - 1) for an input extent m, which is always even: give n to recover an odd length.

axes

The dimensions to transform, 1-based, without repeats. NULL means all of them, in order; for fft_r2c() and fft_c2r() it means all of them in reverse order, so the first dimension is halved. With explicit axes, the real transforms halve the last axis listed, as SciPy does: axes = seq_along(dim(x)) halves the last dimension. Use axes = 1 for a column-wise transform of a matrix, as stats::mvfft() does.

norm

Where the scaling goes, as in fft_c2c(). "ortho" makes the transform orthonormal when orthogonalize is TRUE.

orthogonalize

Whether to scale the first and last terms so that the "ortho" transform matrix is orthogonal. NULL (the default) means norm == "ortho", as in SciPy. For complex input an explicit value is ignored and norm == "ortho" is used, as SciPy does.

workers

Threads to use. NULL uses the session default (1). Negative values count back from the number of available cores: -1 means all of them. Requests are capped at the available cores, and at 2 when _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ is set. Threads split the independent 1-D transforms of a multi-dimensional array, so they help only arrays with at least 32 768 elements and more than one line. Results agree to rounding whatever the number of threads; they are bit-identical on builds without fused multiply-add (CRAN's x86-64 builds).

Value

A double vector or array (complex for complex input) of the same shape as x after cropping or padding to n.

Details

Unnormalised (norm = "backward" or "none" in the forward direction), for a length N, fft_dct() computes

  • type 1: y[k] = x[0] + (-1)^k x[N-1] + 2 sum_{n=1}^{N-2} x[n] cos(pi k n / (N-1))

  • type 2: y[k] = 2 sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] cos(pi k (2n+1) / (2N))

  • type 3: y[k] = x[0] + 2 sum_{n=1}^{N-1} x[n] cos(pi (2k+1) n / (2N))

  • type 4: y[k] = 2 sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] cos(pi (2k+1) (2n+1) / (4N))

and fft_dst() the matching sine sums (type 1 over N + 1, types 2 to 4 as above with sines and indices shifted by one). Type 1 needs lengths of at least 2 for the cosine transform.

inverse = TRUE computes the inverse: types 2 and 3 swap, and the scaling moves to the other direction. With norm = "backward" the inverse is scaled by 1/N, where N is 2(n - 1) for DCT-I, 2(n + 1) for DST-I and 2n otherwise, per transformed axis, so that fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE) returns x.

See also

Other transforms: fft_c2c()

Examples

x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2)
fft_dct(x)
#> [1]  3.000000e+01 -3.863703e+00 -6.928203e+00  1.414214e+00 -8.881784e-16
#> [6] -1.035276e+00
fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 3 2
fft_dst(x, type = 4, norm = "ortho")
#> [1]  6.14884909  2.04209106 -0.84419068  0.38140113  0.40397705 -0.01403076

# an orthonormal DCT-II along the columns of a matrix
m <- matrix(rnorm(12), 4, 3)
fft_dct(m, axes = 1, norm = "ortho")
#>            [,1]        [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] -0.4582745 -0.47284645  0.1321692
#> [2,]  1.9861091  0.09495932  0.2750818
#> [3,]  0.6602879 -0.96324089  1.0737615
#> [4,]  2.4631732  0.49518461 -1.1623026
